newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain's Telefonica drops cable deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain's Telefonica drops cable deal.

text.p: Spanish telecommunications firm Telefonica on Friday announced it was pulling out of its cable venture with Sogecable at the same time as the government said it was freezing the firm's urban tariffs until 1998.
But analysts said the measures should have little effect on the company's share price, backed by strong demand ahead of the sale of the government's remaining 21 percent stake next year.
Telefonica confirmed it would end its Cablevision deal with Sogecable, part of a group including French pay TV giant Canal Plus.
This followed news from Brussels that it was likely to face a European Commission ban on the grounds that it would create a dominant position on the Spanish market.
Analysts said Telefonica's withdrawal from the Cablevision deal had been expected for some time.

"The Sogecable news has no effect. Telefonica owns the network and had a kind of exclusive deal with Canal Plus on possible cable television. If it affects anyone it'll be Canal Plus," said Ignacio Cornejo, an analyst at Beta Capital brokerage.
"Telefonica isn't bothered because anything to do with cable would have to come through its network."
Government confirmation that urban phone charges are to be frozen until June 1998 was also anticipated as part of Spain's drive to combat inflation.

"It's something (Telefonica) had taken into account in its forecasts for the next few years, so it's no surprise. It would have been a suprise if they were cut, as some reports indicated, (as) there would be pressure on the government to cut charges because of the CPI," said an analyst at the Ibersecurities brokerage.
Cornejo agreed the effect of the freeze was neutral.

"The local tariff is being maintained, but it also supposes that metropolitan and provincial calls will be frozen too. These fell when the last adjustments were made (and the local rate rose), so the average rise is quite small or even negative in some cases," he said.
"One has compensated for the other two, and now that they will be held stable, the total effect will be neutral."
A local tariff freeze had already been taken into account in forecasts, analysts said.

"I can't see anything new because in our estimates we forecast a slight increase in 1998 tariffs. So a freeze in 1997 and part of 1998 comes within our expectations," said an analyst at a major domestic bank.

"I even think that Telefonica would have room to cut international tariffs and leave the (local) hike for 1998. The growth in calls per line and from its new services would more than compensate for this," he added.
